posts.title: Amping up T cells to target cancer
posts.summary: Vaccines that turn the body’s immune system against tumors have shown promise in clinical trials, and a handful have been FDA approved for certain cancers. In many patients, however, these vaccines don’t stimulate enough of a response, and the approach some researchers have taken to strengthening it—delivering the vaccine along with immune-stimulating molecules called cytokines—can…
bullets: Researchers have developed a new mRNA-based vaccine adjuvant that significantly amplifies the T-cell response, potentially overcoming the limitations of current cancer immunotherapies.
In preclinical studies, the adjuvant enabled the immune system to slow or eradicate various solid tumors, including melanoma and metastatic lung cancer, even without specific antigen targeting.
The technology also enhances the efficacy of existing FDA-approved checkpoint blockade inhibitors by creating a more T-cell-permissive environment within the tumor microenvironment.

posts.title: A new stamp on cyberfraud prevention
posts.summary: For Rupert Young ’95, SM ’95, his career in data science and cybersecurity began when his grandfather gifted him thousands of stamps: He built intricate databases to catalogue them, displaying the “precise eye” for detail and nuance that his MIT application essay said would make him a good engineer. Young is now chief product officer…
bullets: MaxMind’s GeoIP tool is a critical infrastructure component for streaming services, banks, and e-commerce platforms to verify user locations and prevent cyberfraud.
The service enables real-time decision-making, such as currency adjustment for retail sites and flagging suspicious login attempts based on IP-address data.
As digital fraud becomes more sophisticated, the role of precise, high-resolution geolocation data remains a cornerstone of enterprise-grade security and risk management.

posts.title: Taking your temperature from the inside
posts.summary: Oral and forehead thermometers may not accurately capture a person’s core body temperature, and the few ingestible temperature sensors on the market are so big they are hard to swallow and risk obstructing the GI tract. But MIT engineers created one that can send continuous temperature updates at a size of just six by four…
bullets: MIT engineers have developed a 6x4 millimeter ingestible sensor capable of continuous, high-precision core body temperature monitoring with 0.01 °C accuracy.
The device utilizes a backscattering strategy to minimize power consumption, allowing it to be powered by a small coin cell battery while transmitting data via radio waves to an external antenna.
This technology offers a non-invasive alternative for monitoring immunosuppressed patients, athletes, and individuals in extreme environments, potentially replacing traditional thermometers.

posts.title: Your brain on AI
posts.summary: Many people find AI-based chatbots helpful in keeping up with news, but a study by Pattie Maes and her colleagues at the MIT Media Lab points to a big problem with this strategy.  Participants who evaluated paired news headlines and images over the course of four weeks were initially 21% percent more accurate at telling…
bullets: A study from the MIT Media Lab suggests that reliance on AI-based chatbots for news consumption may negatively impact a user's ability to accurately evaluate information.
Participants in the four-week study showed a significant decline in their ability to correctly identify news accuracy after engaging with AI-curated content.
The findings highlight a critical risk regarding the 'truthfulness' of AI-assisted information gathering and the potential for cognitive degradation in news literacy.

posts.title: China proposes automakers handle traffic violations in fully autonomous mode
posts.summary:
China's draft revision to its road traffic safety law proposes that manufacturers handle traffic violations in fully autonomous driving mode.
For details, please visit CnEVPost (cnev.co).
bullets: A proposed revision to China's Road Traffic Safety Law mandates that automakers assume responsibility for traffic violations committed while a vehicle is in fully autonomous mode.
The regulation creates a legal distinction between fully autonomous driving and assisted driving, with the latter remaining the responsibility of the human driver.
This framework aims to clarify liability as China prepares for the July 2027 implementation of national technical standards for L3 and L4 autonomous driving systems.
